units.t: The Universe. Episode four.
In this episode: Neutron stars and pulsars, Galaxies and the Milky Way, How we measure the universe and Dark matter and dark energy.
Part one. Neutron stars and pulsars.
Imagine squeezing more than the mass of the Sun into a ball the size of a city, then spinning it hundreds of times a second.
City-sized and crushing.
A neutron star is about 1.
4 times the mass of the Sun, yet only around 20 kilometres across, roughly the size of a large city.
A teaspoon of its material would weigh something like a billion tonnes on Earth.
Its surface is thought to be incredibly smooth, with mountains only millimetres tall.
Beneath it, matter is crushed so tightly that most electrons and protons have merged into neutrons.
The core of a massive star fuses elements until it makes iron, which cannot release energy by fusion.
Gravity wins, and the core collapses in a fraction of a second.
The outer layers rebound in a supernova.
A lighter core becomes a neutron star; a heavier one becomes a black hole.
Little green men.
In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a postgraduate student at Cambridge, noticed a bit of "scruff" on chart paper from a new radio telescope.
It was a signal pulsing with astonishing regularity, about every 1.
3 seconds.
The team half jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for "little green men".
More pulsing sources elsewhere made an alien explanation very unlikely.
The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, an omission many scientists consider unfair.
The sources were rapidly spinning neutron stars.
A collapsing core spins faster as it shrinks, like a skater pulling in their arms.
Magnetic fields channel beams of radiation from the poles, and each time a beam crosses Earth, telescopes record a pulse.
The fastest known spins over 700 times a second.
Extreme magnetars.
Some neutron stars have magnetic fields far more extreme than usual.
Magnetars are estimated to have fields up to around a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's.
As a magnetar's crust shifts under these enormous stresses, it can unleash sudden bursts of X-rays and gamma rays.
In December 2004 a giant flare from a magnetar called SGR 1806-20, on the far side of our galaxy, was so powerful that it measurably disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere.
Astronomers now suspect that some magnetars are behind fast radio bursts, brief and extremely energetic flashes of radio waves detected from across the universe.
Collisions that forge gold.
Many neutron stars live in pairs, spiralling slowly towards each other.
In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a binary pulsar whose orbit shrank exactly as Einstein's theory predicts if the pair radiates gravitational waves.
It earned a Nobel Prize in 1993.
On 17 August 2017, detectors caught the gravitational waves of two neutron stars colliding about 130 million light-years away.
Telescopes worldwide, including in Australia, watched the glowing aftermath, called a kilonova.
Its light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements.
Astronomers estimate that mergers like this have produced a significant share of the universe's gold, platinum and other heavy metals, possibly including some of the gold in your jewellery.
Clocks across the galaxy.
Some millisecond pulsars tick with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks.
Australia has played a big role in studying them, and CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope, Murriyang, has discovered a large share of all known pulsars.
By timing dozens of pulsars over many years, astronomers watch for tiny shared shifts in when their pulses arrive.

In 2023, several international teams, including the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, reported evidence of a faint background of very long gravitational waves rippling through the galaxy, likely produced by pairs of supermassive black holes.
Pulsars have even been proposed as a galactic GPS.
The plaques on the Pioneer probes and the Voyager records already carry a map of the Sun's position relative to 14 pulsars, a cosmic return address.
The key idea: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across, left behind when a massive star's core collapses.
Part two. Galaxies and the Milky Way.
On a dark night in outback Australia you can see our own galaxy's glowing core overhead, and two other galaxies with the naked eye.
Our home galaxy.
The Milky Way is a vast system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity.
It is a barred spiral: a central bar of stars inside a flat disc with spiral arms, all wrapped in a faint halo of old stars.
It spans roughly 100,000 light-years and holds perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars.
The Sun sits in a minor arm, the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.
We orbit at about 800,000 kilometres an hour, yet one lap takes around 230 million years.
At the centre lies a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times the Sun's mass.
Because we live inside the disc, we see it edge-on, as a milky band.
"Galaxy" comes from the Greek for milk.
A southern sky advantage.
Australians have one of the best views of our galaxy.
Its brightest part, towards Sagittarius and Scorpius, rides high overhead on winter evenings.
Many Aboriginal cultures trace figures in the dark dust lanes, not just the stars.
The Emu in the Sky has its head in the dark Coalsack beside the Southern Cross, and its body along the Milky Way.
For many groups its position is linked to the emu breeding season, though stories differ between Nations.
Look south on a dark night and you may spot the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, dwarf galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away.
Aboriginal people knew them for thousands of years before Magellan's crew recorded them.
For the best view, try a dark site such as Warrumbungle National Park.
Galaxy shapes.
In the 1920s, astronomer Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by shape, and his scheme is still broadly used.
Spiral galaxies, like ours, have flat discs with arms where new stars form, and many have a central bar.
Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars with little gas for new ones; the largest known galaxies are giant ellipticals.
Lenticular galaxies sit in between, with a disc but no clear arms.
Irregular galaxies have no tidy shape, often because gravity from neighbours has pulled them around.
Collisions between galaxies are common over cosmic time, and they can transform one type into another.
Galaxies that eat galaxies.
Big galaxies grow by merging with smaller ones.
The Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy is being stretched into streams of stars by our gravity right now.
Data from the Gaia spacecraft showed that a sizeable galaxy, nicknamed the Gaia Sausage, crashed into ours 8 to 11 billion years ago.
Many astronomers suspect Omega Centauri, a star cluster easily seen from Australia, is the leftover core of another victim.
Even so, stars almost never hit one another, because the gaps between them are so vast.
The largest galaxy in our Local Group, Andromeda, is about 2.
5 million light-years away and approaching at about 110 kilometres/s.
A 2025 study put the odds of a merger within the next 10 billion years at about 50-50.
Andromeda is visible to the naked eye from the north of Australia.
The dark matter puzzle.
In the 1970s, astronomer Vera Rubin and colleagues measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies.
Stars far from the centre moved just as fast as those closer in, far faster than the visible matter's gravity could hold.
Something unseen was adding gravity.
Astronomers call it dark matter.
It seems to make up about 85 per cent of all matter in the universe, forming huge halos around galaxies.
Nobody yet knows what it is, and a minority of physicists explore modified gravity instead.
Every galaxy you see in the night sky is only the visible part of something much larger.
Let your eyes adjust for 20 minutes under a dark sky and look for yourself.
The key idea: The Milky Way is a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across, holding perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars.
Part three. How we measure the universe.
No one has ever stretched a tape measure to a star, yet we know distances across billions of light-years.
The trick is a ladder of clever steps.
How far is far.
Light covers about 300,000 kilometres every second.
Even so, sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, and light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, takes over four years.
So astronomers use the light-year: the distance light travels in a year, about 9.
5 trillion kilometres.
It is a distance, not a time.
That has a fascinating consequence.
Look at a star a thousand light-years away and you see light that left it a thousand years ago.
Looking further means looking back in time.
No single method works for everything.
Astronomers built a chain of techniques, each checked against the last, called the cosmic distance ladder.
Echoes and parallax.
The first rung is our own neighbourhood.
Knowing the speed of light, we can bounce signals off objects and time the echo.
Radar off Venus, Mars and asteroids fixes the solar system's scale; the Earth to Sun distance, the astronomical unit, is about 150 million kilometres.
Lasers fired at reflectors left by Apollo astronauts give the Moon's distance to within millimetres, and show it drifting away a few centimetres a year.
Next comes parallax.
Hold a thumb at arm's length and look with one eye, then the other: it seems to jump against the background.
Astronomers use two positions of Earth, six months apart.
A nearby star shifts slightly against distant ones, and geometry turns that shift into a distance.
Friedrich Bessel first managed it in 1838; the Gaia spacecraft has since measured over a billion stars.
Leavitt and Hubble.
Parallax only works nearby.
Beyond it, astronomers need standard candles: objects of known true brightness.
In the early 1900s Henrietta Swan Leavitt of Harvard Observatory studied the Small Magellanic Cloud, visible from Australia.
She found that Cepheid variables, stars that brighten and dim rhythmically, follow a pattern: the slower the pulse, the brighter the star.
So a Cepheid's rhythm reveals its distance.
In the 1920s Edwin Hubble used this to settle whether spiral nebulae lay inside the Milky Way.
Cepheids in Andromeda showed it was a separate galaxy far beyond our own, now known to be about 2.
5 million light-years away.
The known universe grew from one galaxy to billions.
Exploding yardsticks.
Cepheids are not bright enough to see in very distant galaxies.
For those, astronomers use Type Ia supernovae.
These are thought to occur when a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star like the Sun, is pushed over a critical limit and blows apart.
Because they explode in a fairly consistent way, their peak brightness can be worked out.
That makes them standard candles visible across billions of light-years.
In 1998 two teams used them to discover that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing down.
One team was led by Brian Schmidt, working at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory near Canberra.
He shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics with Saul Perlmutter and Adam Riess.
Redshift and a puzzle.
At the top of the ladder is redshift.
As the universe expands, light is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths.
The further away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes and the redder its light, a relationship known as Hubble's law.
Once the ladder is calibrated, redshift tells astronomers roughly how far away a galaxy is.
But there is a puzzle.

Measuring today's expansion rate with the ladder of Cepheids and supernovae gives a noticeably higher answer than calculating it from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background.
This mismatch, called the Hubble tension, has persisted as measurements have improved.
It might be a subtle error somewhere, or a sign that our picture of the universe is missing something.
The key idea: Astronomers measure space in light-years, the distance light travels in a year, using a chain of methods called the cosmic distance ladder.
Part four. Dark matter and dark energy.
Everything we have ever seen, every star, planet and person, makes up only about 5 per cent of the universe.
The rest is a mystery with a name but no explanation.
The missing mass.
In 1933 Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured the speeds of galaxies in the Coma Cluster.
They moved so fast that the cluster should have flown apart, unless it held far more mass than its light suggested.
He called the hidden material 'dunkle Materie', German for dark matter.
His estimate was far too large, since distances were badly underestimated then, but the puzzle was real.
In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured spiral galaxies such as Andromeda.
In a solar system, outer planets orbit slowly.
In these galaxies the outer stars did not slow down.
The simplest explanation was a vast, invisible halo of extra mass around each galaxy.
Seeing the invisible.
Dark matter gives off no light, but it has gravity, and gravity bends light.
Massive galaxy clusters act as giant warped lenses, stretching the images of more distant galaxies into arcs.
By measuring that distortion, astronomers can map where the mass actually is.
The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that collided.
In 2006 researchers showed that most of the ordinary matter, hot gas, had been slowed and piled up in the middle.
Most of the mass, revealed by lensing, had passed straight through.
This was widely seen as strong evidence that dark matter is a real substance, separate from ordinary matter.
What could it be.
Dark matter is not simply dim stars, dust or black holes.
Observations rule out ordinary matter making up more than a small fraction of it.
Most physicists think it is a particle outside the standard model of particle physics, one that interacts with almost nothing except through gravity.
Candidates include weakly interacting massive particles, nicknamed WIMPs, and extremely light particles called axions.
Experiments deep underground, shielded from cosmic rays, wait for a dark matter particle to bump into an atom.
Australia's Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory, in a Victorian gold mine, hosts one.
So far there is no confirmed detection, and a minority of scientists suspect gravity itself needs modifying.
A speeding-up universe.
Astronomers have known since the 1920s that the universe is expanding.
The natural assumption was that gravity would slow it.
In the 1990s two rival teams set out to measure the slowdown using Type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs with a predictable peak brightness that work as cosmic distance markers.
Saul Perlmutter led one team in the United States.
Brian Schmidt led the other, the High-Z Supernova Search Team, at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory, with Adam Riess making key analyses.
In 1998 both found the same startling result: distant supernovae were fainter than expected, so the expansion is accelerating.
The three shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Dark energy.
Something seems to be pushing space apart.
Physicists call it dark energy, a name for the effect rather than an explanation.
The leading idea is that empty space carries a small, constant energy, like the cosmological constant Einstein added to his equations and later abandoned.
Yet quantum theory predicts a value wildly larger than observed, one of science's biggest mismatches.
The universe's budget appears to be about 68 per cent dark energy, 27 per cent dark matter and only 5 per cent ordinary matter.
Recent results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument in Arizona hint that dark energy may be weakening, but they are not yet conclusive.
We can measure the universe precisely and still not say what most of it is.
The key idea: Galaxies spin and cluster as if they hold far more mass than their visible stars and gas supply.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is left behind when a massive star's core collapses and the outer layers explode?
Answer. A neutron star or, if heavier, a black hole.
Question two. Why do we see the Milky Way as a band across the sky?
Answer. We live inside its flat disc and look along it edge-on.
Question three. What does it mean to see a star that is a thousand light-years away?
Answer. You see light that left it a thousand years ago.
Question four. What did Vera Rubin find in spiral galaxies?
Answer. Outer stars orbit about as fast as inner ones.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
